# Phase 12 — Replay vs live. Results.

*Generated by `scripts/phase12-results.py` from `validation/replay-vs-live-2019-12-30.json`. Every number here is in that artifact; none is typed.*

The same strategy, the same 150,853 messages of MSFT 2019-12-30, twice: once through the phase-6 queue backtester, once live through the phase-12.7 closed loop over real sockets.

## The two lanes

| | orders | fills | shares |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **lane B — live** | 634 | **847** | 42,939 |
| lane A — `naive` | — | 1,888 | 70,600 |
| lane A — `optimistic` | — | 1,610 | 70,300 |
| lane A — `mbo` | — | 1,281 | 70,000 |
| lane A — `pessimistic` | — | 1,207 | 70,000 |

**Lane B fills less than every model the backtester offers.** The rest of this document is why, and every part of the gap is named.

## Why there is no per-fill diff

The plan says "diff the fills", which presumes a key pairing a lane-A fill with a lane-B fill. There is none, and the reason is a property of the system rather than of the tooling.

**Lane B is not reproducible at the fill level.** `tools/exchange.cpp` polls TCP and then replays *one* message, so which historical message a strategy order lands after is a wall-clock race between two processes. Two runs of the same binaries on the same feed with the same flags gave **617 orders / 880 fills** and **634 / 847**. Phase 12.8 shows the same at scale: chain-A hops pool to n = 12,000 = 10 × 1,200 exactly, while every chain-B hop pools to n = 20,868 over those same ten runs — not divisible by ten.

So the comparison is distributional. That is a weaker claim than the plan wanted and it is the true one.

## Category: latency-model shape

The plan says to set lane A's latency model to the measured hops from lane B. That instruction does not survive `tools/exchange.cpp:560`:

```c
elapsed_replay = (wall_now - wall_start) * multiplier
```

The live lane paces the tape by a multiplier, so its wall-clock latency is multiplied into feed time — at the 1000× every committed real-day run used, 13 µs of real order entry is 13 **milliseconds** of feed time. There is no single honest number. So lane A was swept instead:

| latency ns | `naive` | `optimistic` | `mbo` | `pessimistic` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,888 | 1,610 | 1,281 | 1,207 |
| 13,000 | 1,888 | 1,610 | 1,281 | 1,207 |
| 20,000 | 1,888 | 1,610 | 1,281 | 1,207 |
| 250,000 | 1,888 | 1,610 | 1,281 | 1,207 |
| 1,000,000 | 1,888 | 1,610 | 1,281 | 1,207 |

**Identical across five orders of magnitude.** The two lanes' latency models differ and it **cannot explain any disagreement below**: at this quoting rate even a millisecond is far under the interval between quotes. A confound that was worth worrying about, measured and eliminated rather than argued away.

## Category: structural — lane B has no price-priority fill

`include/itchbook/replay/split.hpp:84` is the whole classification table:

```c
return type == 'E' ? Treatment::Aggressor : Treatment::State;
```

Only `'E'` consults the matcher. A historical order that comes to rest at or through a strategy order is applied to the book and never checked against it. **Lane B therefore has no price-priority fill and no through-print fill at all** — not an approximation of them, none.

Lane A labels every fill with the trigger that caused it (`SimFill::trigger`), so the size of the category is counted:

| lane A model | fills | lock | through | structural | fills without them |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `naive` | 1,888 | 317 | 0 | **16.8%** | 1,571 |
| `optimistic` | 1,610 | 356 | 109 | **28.9%** | 1,145 |
| `mbo` | 1,281 | 652 | 123 | **60.5%** | 506 |
| `pessimistic` | 1,207 | 708 | 126 | **69.1%** | 373 |
| **lane B — live** | **847** | **0** | **0** | — | **847** |

**Sixty per cent of `mbo`'s fills and sixty-nine per cent of `pessimistic`'s come from a path the live loop cannot take.**

## Category: queue approximation

| band over the four models | lane B | verdict |
|---|---:|---|
| as reported, `[1,207, 1,888]` | 847 | **OUTSIDE** |
| structural paths removed, `[373, 1,571]` | 847 | **inside** |

This is the phase's result. **The backtester's band does not contain the live outcome** — and once the fill paths the live loop structurally lacks are removed, **it does**. The queue model is not what the gap was made of.

## Category: inventory and marking

Lane B's strategy sees its own orders on the feed — its own `'A'` came back for **633 of 634** orders — and can therefore quote off a book that contains them. Lane A's book is built from the feed alone and never contains its own orders. Quoting *below* the touch keeps this mostly inert: an order two ticks under the bid does not become the bid unless the market falls to it. It is named here because it is real, not because it was measured to matter.

## Caveats, stated up front as the plan requires

- Neither lane models market impact: the strategy's orders consume liquidity the historical participants never saw, and under the 12.0 hybrid those participants never react to it.
- There is no per-fill join key. Lane B's fill count varies run to run -- two runs of the same binaries on the same feed gave 617 orders / 880 fills and 634 / 847 -- so the comparison is distributional.
- The trigger counters differ: lane B counts book-mutating messages, lane A counts every message, so the same stride puts quotes at different instants.

## What is not established

**The strategies are mirrored, not shared.** `include/itchbook/sim/parity_maker.hpp` reproduces `tools/strategy.cpp`'s rule — buy-only, `bid − offset×tick`, the same crossed-book cap, never cancels — but they are two pieces of code. `tools/strategy.cpp` was left untouched deliberately: its behaviour is what 12.7 proved and 12.8 measured to the nanosecond, and editing it to meet the backtester would invalidate both.

**The trigger counters still differ.** Lane B quotes every N messages that mutated its book; lane A counts every message it saw. The same stride therefore puts quotes at different instants. Calibrating the stride until the order counts matched would have hidden this behind a fitted constant; it is left visible.
